item.title: Gulf nations scramble to prevent Iran war from again hitting their doorstep
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
MANAMA, Bahrain - The looming possibility of U.S. strikes on Iran has been met with weary nervousness in the Persian Gulf, as Gulf officials double down on efforts to break through a U.S.-Iran impasse that they know will leave their region vulnerable. Publicly and privately, leaders in Persian Gulf nations, which bore the brunt of Iranian retaliation because they are home to U.S. bases, are calling for de-escalation as concerns about President Donald Trump's war plans grow. Mediators from Qatar arrived in Tehran on Friday as part of the efforts to negotiate an end to the war, according to a person briefed on the talks, who described the trip as a "last-ditch effort to broker an interim deal between Iran and the U.S." that was happening "in coordination with the U.S." Subscribe to The Post Most newsletter for the most important and interesting stories from The Washington Post. Trump has seemed open to a deal - but also to resuming strikes, according to a separate official briefed on the talks, who spoke on the condition of anonymity because of the sensitivity of the situation. Vice President JD Vance, special envoy Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, Trump's son-in-law and envoy, have been pushing for a deal, the official added, as others - including Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth - appear opposed to it. "The next two days will be crucial in determining how the situation unfolds," said an Iranian official, who like some others interviewed for this story spoke on the condition of anonymity because of the sensitivity of the situation. The Americans, they added, are "seeking a positive breakthrough" ahead of the midterm elections. A White House official said in a statement that the United States is "in a very strong position," pointing to U.S. gains in the Strait of Hormuz and Iran's struggling economy. "Iran has been decimated, and things will go one of two ways; the easy way or the hard way," the official said. "President Trump holds all the cards and will do whatever is best for the United States." Trump, the official said, "has great relationships with all of our Gulf partners, and the U.S. has been in regular contact with all of our regional allies since before Operation Epic Fury." On the ground in the Gulf, there is fear and fatigue as the region once again braces for the possibility of drone and missile strikes after months of relative quiet. In Bahrain, an island nation of 1.69 million that has hosted the U.S. Fifth Fleet for more than 30 years and was targeted by hundreds of Iranian drones and missiles, signs of the previous phases of escalation are still obvious. Damage to equipment and infrastructure at the Fifth Fleet headquarters in Manama, which analysts have put in the hundreds of millions, is evident even from the highway. Restaurants and shops long frequented by military members and their families, the vast majority of whom have been evacuated, are empty. Bahrainis said they have been watching the news nervously. "People are expecting something will happen. We don't want it, but we expect it," said Taha Bhutto, 37, a manager at a car dealership who said that during the first months of the war, he watched as drones and missiles flew overhead. At a supermarket, where prices have surged because of supply chain disruptions linked to diminished traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, the store manager said he is stockpiling food and water for his family in case of an escalation. At a hair salon, where business has plummeted during the war, stylists said they are praying that fighting doesn't kick off again. Many said that their perception of the United States had changed over the course of the war - and that they had believed the Fifth Fleet base would protect them but were disappointed to instead find it becoming a vulnerability. "Trump's decisions have affected the whole region," said Ibrahim, a manager at a supermarket in Bahrain. "We should not have been brought into this chaos. We didn't do anything." Ibrahim, who spoke on the condition that only his first name be used because of concerns about criticizing a Bahraini ally, said that everyone here knows that "a dangerous moment" has arrived. "We know that any outcome will be disastrous - and felt most here," he said. Concerns are especially intense surrounding the targeting of civilian infrastructure in the Gulf, which officials fear could be at risk if Trump follows through on his reported plans to resume attacks on Iran after the U.S. midterm elections. Speaking at an event Wednesday at the Middle East Institute, U.S. Sen. Chris Murphy (D-Connecticut) called those plans, which he said he had been briefed on and included strikes on civilian infrastructure, "insane" and bound to lead to a "devastating escalation." "This is the worst scenario for the region," said Abdulkhaleq Abdulla, an Emirati analyst and a retired political science professor. "The chances for a strike after the election - or maybe even before it - appear to be growing by the day." The United Arab Emirate's Foreign Ministry on Wednesday released a statement saying that there was a "need to intensify diplomatic efforts" and "exercise wisdom and pursue political solutions to contain tensions. Earlier in the week, Omani Foreign Minister Badr Albusaidi called on Gulf nations to form a security pact that includes Iran and Iraq, saying that there has been a "terrible cost" to antagonizing and excluding Iran. Since the war began, Gulf nations - which have long fallen under the U.S. security umbrella - have been bolstering their defenses by ramping up purchases from the U.S. but also looking to other partners, including Turkey and South Korea. Shortages of ballistic missile interceptors (Patriot and Terminal High Altitude Area Defense or THAAD) could leave Gulf nations vulnerable, said Albert Vidal, a research associate at the International Institute for Strategic Studies. But in terms of the lower layers of air defense - the counter-drone systems - Vidal said the Gulf states have a "greater menu of available options" than at the beginning of the conflict in February 2026. One thing that is unclear, he noted, is how many ballistic missiles Iran still has in its arsenal. "The Gulf states are in a lose-lose situation," said Thomas Juneau, a professor at the University of Ottawa whose work focuses on Middle East security issues, noting that global interceptor stocks are running low. Interception rates during the first waves of strikes were higher than anticipated, he said, but Gulf defenses still cannot stop every possible hit. "It's impossible for them to be 100 percent effective," he said, adding that the geography of a country as big as Saudi Arabia - which is also facing attacks by Iran-backed Houthi militants - poses a special challenge. "It is a fantasy to think they could defend it all." item.title: U.S. approves sale of 500 Patriot missiles to Ukraine
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
[Reuters] The United States has approved the sale of 500 Patriot missiles to Ukraine, a critically needed munition for defence against escalating Russian aerial attacks. However, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has warned it could take "several years" for the deliveries to arrive. The US State Department said the advanced PAC-3 interceptor missiles would cost $2.1bn (£1.6bn) and would be "funded entirely" by Kyiv's allies in Europe and Canada. On Friday night Zelensky repeated his calls for the US to speed up the release of its Patriots – the only effective weapon for downing Russia's deadly ballistic missiles. Hundreds evacuated from Russian-occupied Oleshky during rare Ukraine ceasefire G20 'family photo' cancelled after protests over presence of Russian minister In an update on Saturday morning, Zelensky said around 200,000 households in the Dnipro region were left without electricity as well as at least 80,000 households in the Kyiv region following Russian strikes on Friday night. He accused Russia of "deliberately targeting civilian infrastructure every day". The US approved sale of Patriot missiles comes after a row between Zelensky and Donald Trump earlier this month when the US eased sanctions on Russia as part of a deal to secure Russian diesel. The US president stated it was time for Ukraine to get a new leader to strike a deal to end the war with Russia. Moscow launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, having earlier seized Crimea and parts of Donbas in the east. Tensions eased after Zelensky held talks with US envoys in Oslo on 20 October. In Friday's statement, the State Department said "this proposed sale will support the foreign policy and national security objectives of the United States by improving the security of a partner country that is a force for political and economic stability in Europe". It said "Ukraine will pay for this purchase with donations from Canada, Germany, and Norway via the JUMPSTART program and national funds, financed by the European Union's Ukraine Support Loan". The statement said the "principal contractor" would be American company Lockheed Martin, adding that "no US funds are involved in this sale". Meanwhile, at the G20 foreign ministers' meeting European diplomats protested over the presence of Russia's Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov by refusing to stand for an official photograph. The meeting is being hosted in Atlanta by US Secretary of State Marco Rubio. "Let me say this directly to the Russian Foreign Minister: We all know who the aggressor in this war is," UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband told Lavrov at the summit, accusing his government of killing innocent civilians in Ukraine. [BBC] Zelensky said earlier this week that Ukraine had been waiting almost a month for the US to sign off on critical missile supplies that the country was running critically low on. In a post on X late on Friday, he welcomed the US announcement but said Ukraine needed the Patriot missiles "right now". He said Russia was intensifying its attacks on key energy infrastructure ahead of winter with "more than 30 Russian strikes" on "critical parts" of Ukraine's power grid over the past two weeks. Kyiv desperately needs the interceptors but there is a global shortage of the munitions due to their use by the US in its war against Iran. It is not clear what the production schedule will be for the Patriots - but it is understood the order is for new builds rather than existing missiles, meaning there is unlikely to be any kind of rapid delivery to Ukraine. Patriots also have lengthy production times, with only 600 missiles produced per year according to the US Department of Defence. In July, Trump said Washington had "not agreed" to license Ukraine to produce Patriot missiles - three weeks after offering the country such a right. item.title: D.C. and Virginia sue to stop Trump's massive arch days before construction
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
The D.C. government and the state of Virginia sued Saturday to block construction of President Donald Trump's planned triumphal arch, calling it a "flagrantly unlawful" project that will forever change the landscape of the nation's capital. The lawsuit is the latest attempt to stop the 250-foot-tall arch, which Trump hopes to build near Arlington National Cemetery and says will commemorate the nation's 250th birthday. The administration would like to begin construction as soon as next week. Subscribe to The Post Most newsletter for the most important and interesting stories from The Washington Post. The two jurisdictions are asking a federal judge to halt the plan and argue that they have "indisputable standing" to bring their lawsuit because the towering arch would have tangible, negative effects on the region - an argument that distinguishes their lawsuit from others that have tried to stop Trump's construction projects. D.C. Attorney General Brian Schwalb (D) said the arch construction would cause "serious, immediate and irreparable harm to the District and its residents," while Virginia Attorney General Jay Jones (D) said "Trump's illegal vanity project" would be an affront to Arlington National Cemetery and the "extraordinary sacrifices it represents." "The Commonwealth has a solemn duty and a profound interest in preserving the dignity of this sacred place," Jones said in a statement. "We will vigorously litigate to protect its sanctity and honor the legacy of those who made the ultimate sacrifice." The arch already faces legal peril. In a separate case brought by three Vietnam War veterans and a historic preservationist, a federal judge on Friday signaled she might block it. The administration has acknowledged that the arch will unavoidably harm local historic sites by altering views, and that it will divert traffic and create loud noise during years of planned construction, among other disruptions. The Trump administration has tried to defend the arch and the president's other construction projects by claiming that litigants lack standing - the legal grounds to sue - because they cannot show that they would be directly harmed. That argument swayed the Supreme Court this summer in a case about Trump's White House ballroom. The justices ruled 5-4 that a historic preservationist likely could not prove that she would be harmed by the project - and cleared the way for Trump to keep building. D.C. and Virginia say they would suffer "irreparable injuries" if Trump's project proceeds. In their court filing, the jurisdictions argue that the arch would harm the region's security and emergency preparedness, disrupt traffic, degrade the environment and run afoul of the Height Act, which caps building heights at 130 feet in D.C. - a defining feature of the city's architecture intended to preserve views of the Washington Monument and the U.S. Capitol. The arch would be nearly double that height. They also say the arch is illegal because Congress has not authorized it, and because the National Park Service failed to follow laws requiring "appropriate consultation before undertaking a project that would transform the District's physical landscape and upend its historic plan." The Trump administration has said construction could begin by Nov. 5 if the National Capital Planning Commission approves the arch proposal at its meeting that day and the Interior Department greenlights construction. Lawyers for D.C. and Virginia argue that if the court fails to act now, the administration could swiftly shift to a new argument - as officials did last year with Trump's ballroom - that once construction on project begins, it will be too late to stop. "The court should not allow this cynical gambit to succeed," they wrote in the filing. The speed and scope of the president's project - a planned five-level "concrete structure clad in granite," as federal officials have described it - have alarmed historic preservationists, architects, parks advocates and local groups that say its effects on the region would be irrevocable. The arch would permanently disrupt historic architectural designs by competing with the Washington Monument, local officials argue. It would also obstruct the sight line between the Lincoln Memorial and Arlington House, a memorial to Robert E. Lee. The historic preservation officers from both jurisdictions have raised concerns about a lack of review required by law. But the arch would also cause other logistical headaches, D.C. and Virginia officials say, such as year-round construction for two to three years that would temporarily and permanently change traffic patterns on a busy artery. D.C. leaders have not previously sued to block Trump's construction projects, including the ballroom, the changes to the East Potomac golf course and other projects that have drawn complaints. In a hearing Friday in the separate lawsuit seeking to block the arch, U.S. District Judge Tanya S. Chutkan independently raised questions about how the arch would affect traffic patterns and other potential disruptions to the region. An administration lawyer told the judge that he was not prepared to talk about traffic patterns because that issue was not germane to that case. Chutkan questioned what harm would be caused by waiting several months versus beginning construction as soon as next week. "What is the rush to put this arch up?" she asked. item.title: Google could join Trump's $185 billion Golden Dome missile defense project
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
(Bloomberg) -- Alphabet Inc.’s Google is in talks with the US Defense Department to work on a new data security effort underpinning the $185 billion Golden Dome missile defense program, according to people familiar with the matter. Most Read from Bloomberg Binance Estimates $6.3 Billion Hacked in Crypto's Biggest Heist Stocks Slump as Wall Street Gets AI Wake-Up Call: Markets Wrap Google Erases a Record $500 Billion as AI Eats Into Sales Kushner’s Thrive Holdings to Buy ADT for $7.6 Billion in Cash Intel Suffers Worst Stock Drop in Decades on Weak Forecast The Pentagon is standing up a new industry group that aims to secure the data that feeds into military software being built for Golden Dome, said the people, who spoke on condition of anonymity because the matter isn’t public. The group is likely to involve multiple companies working to ensure data that flows into the new command-and-control software is resilient to attacks, such as attempts to cut access to landlines, cell towers and other critical communications infrastructure, the people said. The talks have focused on Google’s data storage, networking and cybersecurity capabilities, one of the people said. Conversations are still early and plans could change, they said. Aalyria Technologies Inc., a networking company spun out from Google, is involved in the consortium, they added. A Pentagon official said that while the office may explore preliminary concepts, no final decision has been made regarding a new consortium or industry participants. Google and Aalyria declined to comment. Golden Dome is President Donald Trump’s marquee defense program to build a layer of defense systems from ground to space that will protect the US from foreign attack. The Golden Dome’s command-and-control layer, which is being developed by a separate group including Anduril, Palantir and SpaceX, is intended to control and connect weapons systems, radars, and other previously siloed systems across the US military. The effort would mark Google’s first publicly known involvement in the Golden Dome program and another sign of how the search engine giant is continuing to lean into national security and defense work. Both the Pentagon’s separate Golden Dome initiatives to pioneer space-based missile interceptors and its command-and-control consortium rely on numerous companies from startups to established primes, unlike past defense programs that have been more typically anchored by a single, large contractor. Google has had a complicated history with defense work. In 2018, thousands of Google employees protested the company’s involvement in a military AI program called Project Maven, citing concerns that the commercial technology would be supporting warfare. Google ultimately didn’t renew the contract. In the years since, however, the company has created a dedicated public sector business and signed deals with the military for AI and cloud capabilities. In April, Google signed an agreement to use its AI models for classified work at the Pentagon, an about-face from its previous stance amid another, albeit smaller, backlash from employees. item.title: FBI questions donors as 2 Dan Sullivans compete in Alaska Senate race
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
ANCHORAGE, Alaska (AP) — The FBI on Friday began reaching out to donors of Dan J. Sullivan asking about potential deception, as federal authorities ramped up their investigation over the U.S. Senate candidate in Alaska who shares a name with the Republican incumbent. An Anchorage-based FBI agent visited a boat dealership in Petersburg, a small fishing community accessible only by air or water where the candidate lives. The agent left a business card for Charles Flint, who told The Associated Press he has known Dan J. Sullivan for years as a respected teacher and musician. The FBI visit came after federal officials confirmed the existence of a criminal probe over the candidate. The U.S. Department of Justice also pushed Friday for a court order to isolate certain Alaska ballots to investigate potential voter confusion . Flint contributed $500 over the summer to what he considered a long-shot campaign, saying he knew Dan J. Sullivan would have expenses and respected him for “throwing his hat in the ring.” Flint said the FBI agent asked his son, who works at the dealership, whether Flint felt he had been “misled” about which candidate he was supporting. “I don’t feel like I’ve been misled at all,” Flint, who has been out of town, told the AP in a telephone interview, adding he had no intention of calling the agent but would “let him waste his time trying to track me down.” “I don’t think there’s any confusion,” he said, adding he intends to rank Democrat Mary Peltola first on his ballot, followed by Dan J. Sullivan. “Everybody knows who the incumbent is.” Alaska U.S. Attorney Michael Heyman told reporters in Anchorage the federal investigation has been ongoing for several months, but recent revelations from The New York Times that Peltola’s campaign appeared to be involved in recruiting retired teacher Dan J. Sullivan have resulted in a “significant surge of law enforcement assets to Alaska.” The developments come just days before Tuesday’s ranked choice general election in a potentially pivotal race in which Peltola, a former congresswoman, is challenging Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan. At a campaign rally in Anchorage on Friday, Peltola again denied any involvement in any plan to place candidates on the ballot to detract from the incumbent senator. She said she was “deeply offended” by the allegations, which she called “garbage” and part of a “smear campaign” to suppress turnout on the eve of the election. “I know I can beat Dan Sullivan. I do not need any help winning this race,” she told a small group of campaign volunteers at an Anchorage aviation museum. ___ Mustian reported from New York. Associated Press reporter Becky Bohrer contributed reporting from Juneau, Alaska. item.title: DOJ warned election workers in all 50 states. Now a judge has stepped in.
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
A federal judge on Friday ordered the Justice Department to stop threatening state and local election officials with criminal prosecution over their handling of disputes about voter qualifications. U.S. District Judge Trina Thompson also ordered the Trump administration to cease demanding that election workers remove voters from statewide rolls, refuse to issue ballots to specific voters or segregate ballots cast in the midterms based on the administration's claims that some voters are ineligible. "Because the public has a paramount interest in ensuring that election officials and workers are able to carry out their work in accordance with federal law and election procedure, and the official day of the Elections is only a couple of days away, the balance of the equities and public interest weigh in Plaintiffs' favor," Thompson wrote. Thompson, a San Francisco-based Biden appointee, issued the temporary restraining order in connection with a lawsuit brought by the Service Employees International Union and other groups. Her directive also requires the DOJ to reach out to any state or local officials who received warnings about possible prosecution and inform them that "demands and threats of prosecution to election officials and workers … have been enjoined." The Justice Department on Thursday sent letters to election workers in all 50 states alluding to possible prosecution if they didn't preserve election records. DOJ did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the judge's broad ruling. Thompson's order effectively enforces a stern warning issued to the Trump administration by another California-based federal judge, David Carter, earlier this week. "These threats must stop," Carter wrote in a ruling that threw out the Justice Department's effort to compel California to set aside any ballots cast by up to 20,000 people federal officials had identified as likely noncitizens. The 9th Circuit Court of Appeals on Friday declined to set aside Carter's order. Thompson's new directive also follows an order by U.S. District Judge James Boasberg, chief of the federal district court in Washington, D.C., to require the Trump administration to provide the list of those 20,000 purported noncitizens to an immigrant advocacy group. Boasberg's order was rooted, in part, on the group's claim that the Trump administration's threats were influencing the conduct of state and local elected officials. item.title: Election forecasters shift 12 more House races toward Democrats before Tuesday
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
It's crunch time. With just days to go until the 2026 midterm elections, Democratic and Republican candidates for the U.S. House of Representatives nationwide are making one last push to persuade voters in their districts — and help their party win or retain control of the chamber on Nov. 3. The stakes are high. President Trump has enjoyed complete Republican control of Congress for the first half of his second term. Flipping the House would give Democrats the power to block parts of the president's agenda, investigate his administration and even impeach him (again) . Historically speaking, a president's party almost always loses seats when voters return to the polls to judge his first two years in office. (The average number lost since World War II? Twenty-six .) Sometimes, the backlash is so pervasive that the president's party loses seats across a wide range of competitive districts — a phenomenon known as a "wave" election. But the past doesn't necessarily predict the future, and Republicans have certain advantages today that they didn't have before. Here's what needs to happen for each party to come out on top. The races to watch The first thing to know about any House election is that while all 435 congressional districts are technically up for grabs, roughly 80% of those contests (representing about 350 seats) are not considered competitive. House incumbents have always had huge advantages: money and name recognition, mostly. But their head start has only widened in recent years as partisan polarization and redistricting have helped make the vast majority of congressional districts "safe" for one party . These days, incumbents tend to focus more on fending off primary challengers. The general election can be a breeze in comparison. As a result, this year's true battleground is relatively small. According to the nonpartisan Cook Political Report's " race ratings ," just 18 contests are genuine "tossups" at this point. Another 18 "lean Democratic," and 17 "lean Republican." There's also a third competitive category that includes 18 seats where Democrats are the "likely" winners, and 14 seats where the same could be said about Republicans. That's 85 competitive districts — again, out of 435. It’s clear from looking at those ratings which party is playing more defense and which is playing more offense — and where. Only 30 Democratic-held seats are considered competitive, and more than half of them (17) are "likely" to remain Democratic, according to Cook. Just four Democratic seats are toss ups. Just three are leaning Republican. In contrast, a full 55 Republican-held seats are considered competitive — and about half of them are tossups (14) or leaning Democratic (13). Geographically, this year's tossups are concentrated in certain kinds of places: Rust Belt districts in states that have swung from party to party in the past (such as Michigan, Pennsylvania and Ohio); Mid-Atlantic suburbs (in states such as New York, Virginia and North Carolina) where Trump has scrambled some of the usual coalitions; and Sun Belt districts (think Florida, Texas, California and Nevada) where Latinos factor heavily. Trump carried many of these areas in 2024 . On Friday, Cook shifted another dozen of its race ratings toward Democrats — part of a pattern that has seen the outlet move a total of 75 race ratings toward Democrats over the last month. “As the House battleground map has expanded, Democrats now have the potential to win their largest majority since 2009. President Donald Trump’s approval rating is underwater even in deep red seats that he won comfortably in 2024, and heavy spending from Republicans doesn’t appear to be moving the needle,” Cook’s House analyst wrote. “While Democrats won’t reach the 257 seats they had following President Barack Obama’s election — a high water mark for them this century — they could surpass the majorities they had following the 2006 and 2018 blue wave cycles.” She went on to project that Democrats “will flip 12 to 25 seats, giving them as many as 240 seats in the House.” Overall, the map gives Democrats more pickup options — which means more paths to a House majority. The path to a Democratic House Senate and governor contests can be quirky — more state-specific and personality-driven. But national dynamics tend to play a larger role in shaping the composition of the incoming House. So it's not just a matter of who has more targets on the board. It's that the board itself tends to tilt to one side or the other, taking most of those targets with it. A recent example was the 2010 midterm election, when impatience with America's slow recovery from the 2008 financial collapse and frustration with President Barack Obama's response helped Republicans gain 64 House seats. Beyond the history of midterm backlash against the president's party, Democrats have two big advantages right now. One is that the current Republican majority is so minuscule — just 219 votes to 214, including an independent who caucuses with Republicans — that Democrats only need a net gain of three seats to win back the House. The other is that the board seems to be tilting in Democrats' favor — assuming the polls are right. Surveys suggest there's one underlying factor pulling the national electorate to the left: dissatisfaction with Trump. According to the data journalists at Silver Bulletin , an average of 60% of Americans currently disapprove of how Trump is handling his job vs. 37% who approve. That puts the president's net approval rating at -23% — near his all-time low. Trump is earning even lower marks on voters' top issue this year: the cost of living . Shortly after he returned to office, roughly equal numbers of Americans approved and disapproved of how the president was handling inflation. But today — as tariffs and the Iran war help drive prices up — 70% disapprove and 25% approve . That's a 45-point gap. President Trump arrives to speak at a campaign rally at F&M Bank Arena on Oct. 10, 2026, in Clarksville, Tenn. AP Photo/Alex Brandon Democrats aren't particularly popular. But for the party in power, it may be hard to overcome this level of dissatisfaction with the status quo. That's why, when pollsters ask their so-called generic ballot question — If an election for U.S. Congress were held today, which party's candidate would you vote for in your district? — Americans are currently giving Democrats a substantial lead of 9 percentage points , on average. Making matters worse for Republicans, that lead has expanded as swing voters who favored Trump in 2024 — including some Latinos and independents — say they're planning to vote Democratic. To put a 9-point lead in perspective, Democrats were leading by an average of 7.5 points on the generic ballot at this point in 2018, with Trump as president and Republican majorities in the House and Senate. On Election Day, they picked up 41 seats and flipped the House. If the polls are right, Democrats might win control of the House again. The path to a Republican House But are the polls right? Recently, Republicans have pointed to some surprising survey results on the Senate side — including Democratic leads in rural red states such as Iowa , Kansas and Nebraska — to argue that pollsters might be misjudging public sentiment. They're not wrong to say the polls have missed in the past. Polling errors are commonplace; they happen in most elections. But they tend to be random and to change directions from one cycle to another . The Trump era has been a little different. In each of the three presidential contests that Trump himself has competed in, the final average of polls conducted before Election Day underestimated Republicans' performance in the popular vote by an average of 3.8 percentage points, according to data journalist Nate Silver . The theory is that a phenomenon called nonresponse bias — in which Democratic voters are more eager or available to respond to pollsters than Republican voters — might have made Democratic support look stronger than it actually was. Pollsters try to adjust for this by weighting their results — that is, using statistical methods to give less weight to respondents who are overrepresented demographically and more weight to respondents who are underrepresented demographically. But it's difficult to predict in advance who will show up on Election Day. This time around, there are signs that rural Republicans are not responding to pollsters in certain states . Could that mean Republican candidates in those places will outperform their polling? Possibly. But experts say it may also mean that rural Republicans are less supportive of the GOP than they were in 2024 — potentially voting Democratic or staying home on Nov. 3. A voter walks toward his polling place. REUTERS / REUTERS After all, there's been virtually no polling bias toward Democrats in Trump era elections when Trump himself wasn't on the ballot. In fact, the polls since 2016 have overestimated Republican support in midterm elections (by an average of 0.2%) and off-year, special and runoff elections (by an average of 1.3%), according to Silver . Either way, pollsters aren't seeing signs of this rural effect in most states — and even if they were, it might make only a minor dent in Democrats' 9-point national lead . Redistricting is the other Republican advantage. House redistricting efforts typically take place every 10 years, after each new census reveals changes in population distribution. But last summer, Trump successfully pushed GOP legislators in Texas to pass new congressional district boundaries five years earlier than normal to help Republicans win five additional House seats in 2026. This kicked off a tit-for-tat cycle that saw nine states adopt new congressional maps for the midterms — some to benefit Democrats, others Republicans. Now that the dust has settled, Cook projects that Republicans could win nine seats because of redistricting (in Alabama, Florida, Louisiana, North Carolina, Ohio, Tennessee and Texas), while Democrats could win five (in California and Utah). If that plays out, it would net the GOP four seats overall. It's not what Republicans initially hoped to gain from gerrymandering. "We're not gonna win all 13 of those redistricted seats. That's correct. We're not," GOP House Majority Whip Tom Emmer of Minnesota told Axios recently . But it's also not nothing. The hope for the GOP is that some combination of polling error and redistricting boost — along with a late influx of hundreds of millions of dollars to help defend districts Trump won in 2024 — will be just enough to preserve their slim House majority. item.title: El-Sayed campaign wants Stevens to stay away after day of back-and-forth barbs
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
TRAVERSE CITY, MICHIGAN — Michigan's Democratic coalition is fragmenting in real time days before a critical Senate election. After it seemed like former primary rivals Abdul El-Sayed and Rep. Haley Stevens might finally appear together, they’re back to sniping at each other. And it could hardly come at a worse moment as Democrats look to unite behind El-Sayed and hold on to a pivotal Senate seat. El-Sayed’s campaign is asking Stevens to stay away from all future campaign events in the closing days of the race, two people familiar with the decision, who were granted anonymity to discuss sensitive campaign dynamics, told POLITICO. She should stay away “as not to distract from the central issues of the campaign,” one of the people said. The brushoff capped a day of the two lobbing increasingly pointed statements back and forth at each other, frustrating Democrats who say the infighting risks imperiling a state the party can hardly afford to lose as they try to flip control of the Senate. “I have no idea what the hell Haley Stevens is doing. This is a moment where we have to recognize the stakes,” Michigan state Sen. Mallory McMorrow, who was squeezed out of the Democratic primary by the two other candidates, told CNN earlier on Friday, before El-Sayed issued his response. “People are not talking about ads. They are not talking about Haley Stevens. They are talking about the price of gas and groceries.” Stevens did not immediately respond to a question on if she will now stay off the trail, and did not respond to an earlier question about whether her appearance was contingent on him apologizing. El-Sayed’s campaign declined to comment. El-Sayed narrowly defeated Stevens in a bitter and hard-fought primary in August that exposed division over support for Israel. The seat now held by the retiring Democratic Sen. Gary Peters is crucial to Democratic hopes to take control of the Senate. Stevens and El Sayed have not campaigned together since a post-primary unity breakfast, but appeared on the verge of doing so earlier on Friday. Stevens initially said she would appear alongside El-Sayed and South Carolina Rep. Jim Clyburn at a church in Detroit on Sunday. But she said she expected the Democratic nominee to apologize for some of his past comments and condemn an ad run by an outside group supporting him that she described as antisemitic. The ad featured a conversation in a grocery store where a woman told a man they couldn't buy eggs because they had to set aside money for “killing Palestinians.” El-Sayed’s campaign had previously noted he was not affiliated with the ad. In response, El-Sayed did not touch on the ad or his past comments on Israel, instead saying that his campaign “has always been focused on addressing the most critical challenges Michiganders are facing” and that that focus “is why our people-powered campaign defeated a historic $70 [million] in outside spending from big corporations and AIPAC on behalf of Congresswoman Stevens.” “So while Congresswoman Stevens seems intent on relitigating a primary that ended three months ago, let’s all focus on the task at hand: that’s beating Mike Rogers,” El-Sayed said. Privately, Democrats are frustrated — some with Stevens. “Every Democrat was singing the same tune but now, because one person is tone deaf, the whole choir is thrown off,” said a Michigan Democratic operative who is not directly working for El-Sayed’s campaign. Some Democrats tried to downplay the fight heading into the final days of the race. “There’s been a lot of efforts to coalesce Democrats, both from Abdul and from the congresswoman. I think everybody's on the same page of Democrats just beating Mike Rogers," said Joe Tate, a state representative from Detroit who supported Stevens in the primary and is now backing El-Sayed. But he acknowledged that "when you have people that have competed through a primary, I know it can always have those lingering effects." Former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg urged Democrats to come together to support El-Sayed. “I've never met somebody who I agree with on 100 percent of everything,” Buttigieg told reporters while campaigning in the state for House candidate Callie Barr on Friday. “But when our health care is at stake, when a chance to have a more affordable everyday life is at stake, the choice is clear: Mike Rogers has disqualified himself.” Republicans have sought to play up the Democratic divisions. Rogers, in a Friday evening post on X , called Stevens a “courageous leader” and said she was “absolutely right” to call on El-Sayed to apologize. “I agree with her and my campaign is about being there, showing up and defending these communities and all Michiganders,” Rogers said. President Donald Trump, at a Friday night rally in Daytona, Florida, had a characteristically blunt message: "If you're Black, or if you're Jewish, and you vote for Abdul, you're not smart,” he said. Stevens’ comments so close to the pivotal election left some Democrats wondering what her goal was. “If you are someone with a large platform — whether you are, say, an outgoing member of Congress or an out-of-state streamer — who genuinely wants Abdul El-Sayed to become the next U.S. Senator from the state of Michigan and for Democrats to take back the Senate and put a meaningful check on Donald Trump, before you speak publicly I would implore you to ask yourself ‘is what I’m doing actually helping, or am I just seeking attention?’,” Democratic operative Adam Carlson, who has polled for a pro El-Sayed super PAC, wrote on X . Sophia Cai contributed to this report. This article originally appeared on Politico at https://www.politico.com/news/2026/10/30/el-sayed-stevens-senate-race-fight-01144423
